title: How to Write Skilled Nursing Notes in Home Health, With Examples
summary: How to write a skilled nursing note in home health: what it must establish, a full example visit note, why notes come back from QA, and what wording can safely repeat.
body_markdown:
A skilled nursing note has to show what you did, why it needed a nurse, how the patient responded and what happens next. Below is what the note needs to establish, a full example visit note, the gaps that most often send notes back from QA, and how to save the wording that genuinely repeats without saving the findings.


## How to write a skilled nursing note


A skilled nursing note answers the questions a reviewer or the next nurse will ask: what service you provided, why it required nursing skill, how the patient responded, and where they stand against the goals in the plan of care. For Medicare home health, it also includes patient-specific findings that support homebound status, alongside the assessment, interventions and follow-up from this visit.


Answering them is harder than it sounds at a routine visit where most findings match the last one, because the note still has to show why the patient needed a nurse. Unchanged findings belong in the note when you have assessed them, but the note depends on the reasoning around them.


Gaps in that reasoning can send a note back from QA for clarification, adding another task after the visit. A consistent structure helps, adapted to your agency’s requirements and the applicable payer’s rules. It also makes clear which wording genuinely repeats from visit to visit, so you can save it and focus on documenting this visit’s details.


## What a skilled note needs to establish


A diagnosis alone does not explain skilled need. Heart failure tells a reviewer what the patient has, not why this visit required a nurse. The note has to connect the service to the finding, risk or learning need that called for nursing judgment. That service might involve skilled observation and assessment, teaching, management and evaluation of the care plan, or a hands-on procedure.[Medicare guidance](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/bp102c07.pdf) explains these types of skilled care. Skilled care can also maintain a condition or prevent deterioration. Improvement is not a condition of coverage.


Homebound status has two criteria. First, illness or injury must make assistance, a supportive device or special transportation necessary to leave home, or leaving must be medically contraindicated. Second, the patient must normally be unable to leave, and leaving must require considerable and taxing effort. The same guidance allows qualifying absences, including medical care and certain short or infrequent outings.


In a visit note, the criteria are the test, not the evidence. Restating them shows you know the rule but says nothing about this patient. The evidence is the functional detail you assessed today, even when it is unchanged.


The[home health record rules](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-484/subpart-C/section-484.110) require interventions and responses, plus goals and progress, to be documented in the record. Entries must be legible, clear, complete, dated, timed and appropriately authenticated. Your EHR may capture some required information in fixed fields rather than the narrative. The narrative earns its place by connecting findings, care and response.


## Home health skilled nursing visit note examples


The note below shows the structure in full, and the QA section returns to it for shorter examples. This order can help you organize the note:


- **Visit:** the purpose of the visit under the plan of care.
- **Since last visit:** relevant symptoms, falls, emergency visits, hospitalizations or medication changes.
- **Assessment:** measurements against applicable ordered parameters, focused findings and relevant unchanged findings.
- **Intervention and response:** interventions, teaching, what the patient or caregiver demonstrated, and any communication or follow-up.
- **Skilled need and homebound support:** why nursing skill was needed and the patient-specific findings supporting homebound status.
- **Plan for next visit:** what to reassess or follow up, based on today’s findings and response.


This fictional routine RN visit follows a heart-failure hospitalization. Findings and orders are invented, informed by the American Heart Association’s guidance on[symptom monitoring](https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/heart-failure/warning-signs-of-heart-failure/managing-heart-failure-symptoms) and[daily weighing](https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/heart-failure/living-with-heart-failure-and-managing-advanced-hf/physical-changes-to-report-for-heart-failure) . Parameters apply only to this scenario. LPNs should work within their scope of practice and supervision requirements.


### Fictional RN visit note


**Visit:** \[date\], \[start–end time\]. RN follow-up for cardiopulmonary assessment and weight-monitoring education under the plan of care following recent heart-failure hospitalization.


**Since last visit:** Patient reports no falls, emergency visits, medication changes, chest pain or new shortness of breath. Shortness of breath walking from bedroom to kitchen remains unchanged and resolves with seated rest. Patient recorded weight on one of the past three mornings and cannot explain when to call about an increase.


**Assessment:** BP 118/72 mm Hg seated, pulse 78/min regular, respirations 18/min, temperature 98.2°F, SpO₂ 96% on room air. Readings within ordered notification parameters. Patient reports weighing 174.2 lb on home scale this morning, not yet entered in log. Previous visit weight 174.0 lb. Timing relative to breakfast and urination and consistency of clothing not verified, limiting comparison. Lungs clear bilaterally, no shortness of breath at rest, bilateral 1+ ankle edema unchanged. Medication bottles reviewed against current medication list, with no discrepancies identified.


**Intervention and response:** Assessed respiratory status, edema and available weight information. No new signs of worsening fluid retention identified. Reviewed the prescribed daily-weight plan and demonstrated use of the log. Patient initially planned to weigh after breakfast. Following explanation, correctly described weighing after urinating and before breakfast, using the same scale and similar clothing. Patient entered today’s reported reading in the log without prompting and identified the written instruction to call the agency for a gain of 2 lb in 24 hours or 5 lb in a week. Reviewed reporting of new or worsening symptoms. Patient correctly identified increased shortness of breath and swelling as reasons to contact the agency promptly.


**Skilled need and homebound support:** Continued RN assessment and individualized teaching needed following hospitalization because weight monitoring remains inconsistent and reporting instructions required reinforcement. Patient uses walker and another person’s assistance to negotiate entrance steps. Normally leaves only for medical appointments. Walking to the vehicle causes shortness of breath requiring seated rest before travel.


**Plan for next visit:** Reassess cardiopulmonary findings and edema, review daily weight entries and weighing method, and ask patient to apply the reporting instructions to a sample weight change. Reassess whether further teaching is needed. \[Clinician signature/credentials and authentication date/time\].


The ankle swelling is unchanged, and how the weight was taken limits the comparison. The reason for a nurse is in “Since last visit”: the patient logged one weight in three days and cannot say when to call. The rest of the note follows those two gaps. The teaching entry records the misunderstanding and the correction. The skilled-need line rests on the same gaps rather than the diagnosis. At the next visit, the plan reviews the home weight log and weighing method, and asks the patient to apply the reporting instructions to a sample weight change. Learning during one visit is not yet an established routine at home.


**What can repeat:** the visit-purpose frame, the wording of weighing instructions, and the shape of the homebound and next-visit lines. Your name and credentials can be saved too, but each entry still needs authentication. Reuse teaching wording only for teaching actually given, and check reporting thresholds against current orders.


**What comes from today:** measurements, findings, functional limitations, clinical reasoning and what the patient said or demonstrated. That includes findings that are unchanged but were reassessed.


## Why notes come back from QA


Several of the clinical documentation gaps below share a pattern: the note states a conclusion, such as skilled need, homebound status or completed teaching, without the evidence behind it. Before signing, read the entry as a reviewer or the next nurse would. The corrected lines below draw on the fictional visit above.


- **Vague skilled need:** Replace “SN required” with the service and its patient-specific rationale: “Continued RN assessment and individualized teaching needed following hospitalization because weight monitoring remains inconsistent and reporting instructions required reinforcement.”
- **Generic homebound wording:** Replace “taxing effort” alone with functional detail: “Patient uses walker and another person’s assistance on entrance steps. Normally leaves only for medical appointments. Walking to the vehicle causes shortness of breath requiring seated rest.”
- **Teaching without a response:** Replace “Education provided” with the observed result: “Following teaching, patient correctly described when and how to weigh and entered today’s reported reading in the log without prompting.” Document misunderstandings too. A statement of understanding is not the same as teach-back.
- **A finding with no action or follow-up:** Explain your response to a reading outside ordered parameters or a concerning change, including notification and the advice received or follow-up still pending. The[care-planning rules](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-484/subpart-B/section-484.60) require the agency to promptly alert the relevant practitioner to changes suggesting unmet outcomes or a needed plan revision. Urgency depends on the clinical situation. The fictional visit had no such finding, but the notification frame in the next section shows one way to record it.
- **Care that does not match orders:** Check the intervention against current orders and record relevant clarification. The same rules cover following orders.
- **An unclear next step or incomplete entry:** Make the follow-up specific, as the fictional plan does. Check date, time and authentication in the appropriate EHR fields before signing.
- **Outdated copied text:** Remove findings or completed actions that were not established today. Resolve contradictions between the narrative and structured fields.


## Faster notes that still describe this patient


When unfinished notes follow you home, retyping familiar sentences adds to pajama time, and carrying the last note forward can look like a shortcut. A phrase bank offers a different one. It saves the wording that genuinely repeats without saving the findings, leaving more attention for the assessment and decisions you need to explain.


If you already use dot phrases or a personal cheat sheet, the approach is familiar. Save a few frames in your own words, with blanks for this visit’s details:


- **Teaching:** “Teaching addressed \[topic\] using \[method\]. Patient response: \[what they said or demonstrated\]. Follow-up: \[remaining need or next step\].”
- **Homebound support:** “Leaving home: \[assistance/device needed, or why leaving is medically contraindicated\]. Usual ability to leave: \[details\]. Effort involved: \[specific limitations\].”
- **Notification:** “Contacted \[practitioner\] at \[time\] about \[finding\]. Response: \[advice/orders or awaiting reply\]. Follow-up: \[action and responsibility\].”
- **Next visit:** “Reassess \[finding or skill\] to determine \[clinical question or progress toward goal\].”


Use only the frames that fit the encounter. They can sit alongside your EHR’s templates.


In its[electronic-record guidance](https://www.cgsmedicare.com/partb/pubs/news/2012/0812/cope19795.html) , Medicare contractor CGS warns that cloned documentation lacks individual information supporting medical necessity. Although the guidance was written for Part B records, its emphasis on documenting the patient at the time of the encounter is a useful test for saved wording.


That test is why normal findings, symptom denials and completed actions stay out of saved defaults. Take the fictional patient’s edema. “Bilateral 1+ ankle edema unchanged” may be accurate again next visit, but only if the nurse assesses it again. A saved sentence can repeat the words. It cannot establish what you assessed today.
